offline.heading: Your voice never leaves your Mac.
offline.body: Recording, transcription and pasting all happen on the speech model on your disk. There is no server to send anything to, so nothing is sent.

facts.title: No audio leaves
facts.body: The model runs on your Mac, on its own graphics chip.

facts.title: No text leaves
facts.body: What you say goes to the app you are typing in. Nowhere else.

facts.title: No account
facts.body: Nothing to sign up for, and nothing to log in to.

offline.footnote: Two optional things use the network, and neither is about you: downloading a speech model once, and a daily check for updates that you can turn off.

features.heading: Built for people who write all day.
features.lede: Everything below is in the free version. There is no other version.

items.title: Words while you speak
items.body: Live modes type the words into your app as you talk, instead of making you wait for the end.

items.title: A short wait at the end
items.body: When you stop, Nivi only transcribes the part it has not done yet. Even after a long stretch, the finish is quick.

items.title: Your words, fixed for good
items.body: Names and terms the model keeps getting wrong are replaced automatically, every time.

items.title: The right microphone, every time
items.body: List your microphones in the order you prefer. Nivi uses the first one that is plugged in.

items.title: History that stays home
items.body: Every dictation is kept on your Mac, so you can find something you said last week. You choose how long.

items.title: A panel or the notch
items.body: Watch the recording in a small panel near the bottom of the screen, or in a thin bar that merges with the MacBook notch.

hebrew.heading: Hebrew is not an afterthought here.
hebrew.body: Nivi was made by someone who dictates in Hebrew every day. The ivrit-ai model, trained on Hebrew speech, is the default for Hebrew and is far better at it than the general models. Saved files keep Hebrew on the right, where it belongs.

items.a: Yes. Every feature is in the one version there is, and the code is open under the MIT licence.

items.q: Does anything I say leave my Mac?
items.a: No. Audio and text stay on your Mac. The only network use is downloading a model once and an optional daily update check, which sends nothing about you.

items.q: Why does macOS warn me the first time I open it?
items.a: Nivi is signed by its author, not yet checked by Apple, which costs $99 a year. macOS blocks it once and may call it damaged. It is not. The install guide shows the fifteen seconds of clicking that gets past it, and you only do it once.

items.q: Which Macs does it run on?
items.a: Macs with Apple Silicon (M1 or newer) on macOS 14 or newer. You also need disk space for the model you choose: about 1.6 GB for the large models, about 400 MB for the small English one.

items.q: Which languages can I dictate in?
items.a: About a hundred, through Whisper models. Hebrew gets the ivrit-ai model by default. You choose the model for each language.
Into whatever app you are typing in, as if you had typed it. It also goes into a history on your Mac, kept for as long as you choose.

items.q: How do I start and stop?
items.a: Out of the box, double-tap the right Command key to start and tap it once to stop and paste. Press Esc to cancel. You can change all three.

items.q: Which permissions does it need, and why?
items.a: Microphone, to hear you. Accessibility, to paste into other apps and notice your hotkey. Input Monitoring, to notice Esc when you cancel.

profiles.lede: A profile is a hotkey, a speech model, a language and a way of typing. Make as many as you need. The key you press picks the profile.

files.heading: Recordings in. Documents out.
files.lede: Drop in an interview, a lecture or a voice memo. Nivi turns it into paragraphs on your Mac, and saves it in the format you need.
paragraphs: Thanks for making the time. I want to start with how the project began, and why we chose to build it ourselves.
It started as a side project. Within a month, half the team was using it every day, and that told us we should take it seriously.
